pythagorean-theorem.name: Pythagorean theorem
pythagorean-theorem.oneLiner: The theorem that in a right triangle the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides
pythagorean-theorem.description: The Pythagorean theorem states that the square of the hypotenuse of a right triangle equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. It is the most basic theorem of Euclidean geometry and the foundation of the notion of distance. With thousands of known proofs, it is the most studied theorem in the history of mathematics.
pythagorean-theorem.significance: It supplies the definition of Euclidean distance and underlies trigonometry, analytic geometry, vector spaces, and much of modern mathematics.

a.description: The length of one of the sides that meet at the right angle.

b.description: The length of the other side that meets at the right angle.

c.description: The length of the longest side, the one opposite the right angle.

a^2+b^2.role: Sum of the squares of the legs
a^2+b^2.description: The squares of the two leg lengths added together.

c^2.description: The hypotenuse length squared. It equals the sum of the squares of the legs.

heron-formula.name: Heron's formula
heron-formula.oneLiner: The formula for the area of a triangle from the lengths of its three sides alone
heron-formula.description: Heron's formula computes the area of a triangle from its three sides a, b, c and its semiperimeter s. Because you never have to find the height, it is very practical in surveying and whenever you are given coordinates. It has the elegant structure of the squared area written as a product of the semiperimeter and its differences from each side.
heron-formula.significance: Because it gives the area from side lengths alone, with no height needed, it is widely used in surveying and computer graphics.

a.description: The length of the triangle's first side.

b.description: The length of the triangle's second side.

c.description: The length of the triangle's third side.

s.description: Half the sum of the three sides. s = (a+b+c)/2.

A.description: The area of the triangle, computed as sqrt(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)).

circle-area.name: Area of a circle
circle-area.oneLiner: The formula that gives the area of a circle as pi times the radius squared
circle-area.description: The area formula for a circle states that the area covered by a circle of radius r equals pi times the radius squared. Ever since Archimedes proved it by cutting the circle into infinitely thin triangles, it has stood as the prototype of integration.
circle-area.significance: It is the most basic area formula for a curved figure and the historical starting point of the idea of the integral.

A.description: The area the circle covers. Units: length squared.

\\pi.description: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. About 3.14159.

r.description: The distance from the centre of the circle to its edge.

r^2.description: The radius squared. It sets the size of the area.

law-of-cosines.name: Law of cosines
law-of-cosines.oneLiner: The law that gives one side of any triangle from the other two sides and the angle between them
law-of-cosines.description: The law of cosines states that the square of one side of a triangle equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides minus twice their product times the cosine of the included angle. It generalises the Pythagorean theorem: when the included angle is a right angle the cosine is 0 and it reduces to the Pythagorean theorem.
law-of-cosines.significance: It lets you relate sides and angles in any triangle, not just right ones, and it is essential to surveying and navigation.

a.description: The side whose length the law of cosines is being used to find.

b.description: The length of one known side of the triangle.

c.description: The length of the other known side of the triangle.

C.description: The angle between side b and side c.

\\cos C.description: The cosine of the included angle C. It is 0 when the angle is a right angle.

sphere-volume.name: Volume of a sphere
sphere-volume.oneLiner: The formula giving the volume of a sphere as proportional to the cube of its radius
sphere-volume.description: The volume formula for a sphere states that the space taken up by a sphere of radius r is (4/3) times pi times the radius cubed. Archimedes found this relation by inscribing a sphere in a cylinder; it can also be derived by integration, and it is a basic result of three-dimensional geometry.
sphere-volume.significance: It is the most basic volume formula for a curved solid in three-dimensional space and is used widely in physics and engineering.

V.description: The amount of space the sphere takes up. Units: length cubed.

\\frac{4}{3}.description: The factor relating the volume of a sphere to the cube of its radius.

\\pi.description: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. About 3.14159.

r.description: The distance from the centre of the sphere to its surface.

r^3.description: The radius multiplied by itself three times. It reflects how volume grows in three dimensions.

euler-polyhedron.name: Euler's polyhedron formula
euler-polyhedron.oneLiner: The relation between the numbers of vertices, edges, and faces of a convex polyhedron
euler-polyhedron.description: Euler's polyhedron formula reveals the striking fact that for any convex polyhedron, the number of vertices minus the number of edges plus the number of faces always comes to 2. It marked the beginning of topology: however the shape of the polyhedron changes, this relation does not. It is the most basic instance of the topological invariant known as the Euler characteristic.
euler-polyhedron.significance: It was the first result to put a number on a topological property of a geometric object, and it is the starting point of topology and graph theory.

V.description: The total number of vertices (points where edges meet) of the polyhedron.

E.description: The total number of edges (segments where two faces meet) of the polyhedron.

F.description: The total number of faces (flat polygons) of the polyhedron.

2.description: The Euler characteristic of a convex polyhedron (topologically a sphere). It is always 2.

realWorldExamples: Checking a cube: 8 vertices - 12 edges + 6 faces = 2
Checking a football (truncated icosahedron): 60 vertices - 90 edges + 32 faces = 2

circle-equation.name: Equation of a circle
circle-equation.oneLiner: The equation describing a circle on the coordinate plane by its centre and radius
circle-equation.description: The equation of a circle gives the condition satisfied by every point (x, y) on a circle with centre (a, b) and radius r. It follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem and is the basic tool for handling circles algebraically in analytic geometry. Expanding it gives the general form, and completing the square brings it back to the standard form.
circle-equation.significance: It is the central example of analytic geometry's project of writing geometric figures as algebraic equations, and it is essential for analysing how circles and lines relate.

x.description: The horizontal coordinate of any point on the circle.

y.description: The vertical coordinate of any point on the circle.

a.description: The horizontal coordinate of the circle's centre.

b.description: The vertical coordinate of the circle's centre.

r.description: The distance from the centre of the circle to its edge.

realWorldExamples: In GPS positioning, the set of possible locations lying a fixed distance from a given base station
Modelling the reach of a robot arm as the equation of a circle to work out its working area

ellipse-equation.name: Equation of an ellipse
ellipse-equation.oneLiner: The equation for the locus of points whose distances to two foci add to a constant
ellipse-equation.description: The equation of an ellipse gives the condition satisfied by every point on an ellipse centred at the origin with semi-major and semi-minor axes a and b. It generalises the equation of a circle to the case where the x and y axes are scaled differently, and when a = b it becomes a circle. It plays a central role in Kepler's laws of planetary motion.
ellipse-equation.discoverer: Apollonius (in his work on conic sections)
ellipse-equation.significance: It is the mathematical model of planetary orbits, and it has many other applications, from reflective properties in optics to whispering galleries in architecture.

x.description: The horizontal coordinate of any point on the ellipse.

y.description: The vertical coordinate of any point on the ellipse.

a.description: Half the length of the ellipse's horizontal (major) axis. The distance to the farthest point.

b.description: Half the length of the ellipse's vertical (minor) axis. The distance to the nearest point.

a^2.description: The normalising denominator of the x term.

b^2.description: The normalising denominator of the y term.

realWorldExamples: Kepler's first law: a planet traces an elliptical orbit with the Sun at one focus
Whispering galleries: in an elliptical room, sound from one focus gathers at the other

hyperbola-equation.name: Equation of a hyperbola
hyperbola-equation.oneLiner: The equation for the locus of points whose distances to two foci differ by a constant
hyperbola-equation.description: The equation of a hyperbola gives the condition satisfied by every point on a hyperbola centred at the origin with semi-transverse and semi-conjugate axes a and b. Unlike an ellipse, it is the difference of the distances that stays constant, and the curve is open, splitting into two branches. It draws ever closer to the asymptotes y = (b/a)x and y = -(b/a)x without ever meeting them.
hyperbola-equation.discoverer: Apollonius (in his work on conic sections)
hyperbola-equation.significance: It is used in navigation (the LORAN system), in the design of hyperbolic cooling towers, and in the spacetime structure of special relativity.

x.description: The horizontal coordinate of any point on the hyperbola.

y.description: The vertical coordinate of any point on the hyperbola.

a.description: The distance from the centre to a vertex of the hyperbola.

b.description: Half the length of the axis that sets the slope of the asymptotes.

a^2.description: The normalising denominator of the x term.

b^2.description: The normalising denominator of the y term.

realWorldExamples: LORAN navigation: fixing a position from the difference in arrival times of signals from two stations
Hyperbolic cooling towers: a shape that optimises structural strength and airflow efficiency
